title: Electrostatics and Magnetism
scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT Physics, Mathematics and Research Reasoning lessons. Models and calculations use stated assumptions. Independent scientific review is pending; this is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: Electric charge is conserved and occurs in integer multiples of the elementary charge for ordinary isolated particles. A neutral object has balanced positive and negative charge, not an absence of charged constituents.
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charging by contact redistributes charge; polarization separates charge within an initially neutral object.
In ordinary solid conductors, mobile electrons move while positive lattice ions remain approximately fixed. Conventional positive-current direction need not match electron drift.
An isolated conductor can redistribute its charges without changing total charge. Grounding permits charge exchange with a much larger reservoir.

steps.text: For point charges in vacuum, Coulomb-force magnitude is k|q1q2|/r². The force lies along the line joining the charges.
Superposition adds the forces from several sources as vectors. Cancellation depends on direction, not merely on equal magnitudes.
Doubling separation divides force by four when the charges and medium are unchanged. The inverse-square law concerns center-to-center separation in the point-charge approximation.
Electric field is force per positive test charge: E = F/qtest. Changing the test-charge sign reverses its force relative to the field but does not reverse the source field.

steps.text: For two point charges in vacuum with zero energy at infinite separation, electric potential energy is U = kq1q2/r. Its sign depends on the signed charge product.
Like-charge pairs have positive U in this convention; opposite-charge pairs have negative U. A negative potential energy is compatible with a stable choice of zero at infinity.
For an electrostatic field, work done by the field equals -ΔU. External quasistatic work with no kinetic-energy change equals +ΔU.
Potential energy belongs to a charge configuration, not to position alone. Changing the moving charge changes its energy even if the source potential is unchanged.

steps.text: Electric potential is potential energy per charge: V = U/q. A potential difference has units joules per coulomb, called volts.
A charge moving across ΔV changes electric potential energy by qΔV. A negative charge reverses the energy-change sign relative to a positive charge.
For a uniform one-dimensional field, Ex = -ΔV/Δx. The field points toward decreasing potential, while force direction also depends on the sign of the charge.
Equipotential surfaces require no electrostatic work for motion along them. Zero potential at a point does not necessarily imply zero electric field there.

steps.text: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside conducting material is zero. This statement does not apply to every cavity containing an internal charge or to a current-carrying conductor.
An equilibrium conductor is equipotential, and excess charge resides on its surface. Surface charge distribution depends on geometry and nearby charges.
A dipole has separated opposite charges and zero net charge. Its far field is not zero everywhere simply because the total charge is zero.
A uniform external field can exert a torque on a dipole without a net translational force. A nonuniform field can also produce a net force.

steps.text: A moving point charge in a magnetic field experiences F = qv × B, with magnitude |q|vB sin θ. A charge at rest has no magnetic force from this term.
For a positive charge, use the right-hand rule for v × B; reverse the force for a negative charge. The magnetic field direction is not generally the force direction.
A magnetic force perpendicular to velocity changes direction without changing speed when it is the only force. It does no work on an ideal point charge.
A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field. The field around a long straight wire circles it according to the right-hand rule for conventional current.
